ripple_effect.name: Natural disaster hitting a manufacturing hub

historical_precedents.event: Japan's Tōhoku earthquake, tsunami, and Fukushima nuclear disaster
historical_precedents.what_happened: The disaster killed thousands of people and forced widespread factory shutdowns across Japan, which was and remains a major supplier of automotive parts and specialized electronic components.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Global automakers, including outside Japan, had to slow or halt production for weeks due to parts shortages, and some categories of electronic components saw temporary global shortages and price increases.

historical_precedents.event: Thailand floods
historical_precedents.what_happened: Months of monsoon flooding submerged major industrial estates north of Bangkok that housed a large share of the world's hard-disk-drive manufacturing along with numerous automotive-parts factories, forcing an extended shutdown of dozens of plants.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Global hard-drive prices roughly doubled for several months due to the shortage, and several Japanese automakers had to cut production at plants worldwide because of parts sourced from the flooded factories.

possibility_chains: A natural disaster affecting a region that supplies a specialized, hard-to-substitute component has historically caused production disruptions for manufacturers worldwide, not just locally, given how concentrated some supply chains are geographically.

Disruptions of this kind have historically prompted affected companies to review and diversify their supplier base over the following months and years, though meaningful diversification has typically taken longer than the disruption itself.

Recovery timelines have historically depended heavily on how specialized and geographically concentrated the affected manufacturing capacity was — highly specialized hubs (e.g. certain semiconductor fabrication) have taken longer to recover than more easily relocated production.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Thailand floods (July–November 2011): Global hard-drive prices roughly doubled for several months due to the shortage, and several Japanese automakers had to cut production at plants worldwide because of parts sourced from the flooded factories. A natural disaster affecting a region that supplies a specialized, hard-to-substitute component has historically caused production disruptions for manufacturers worldwide, not just locally, given how concentrated some supply chains are geographically.

ripple_effect.name: Coup or abrupt regime change disrupting trade relationships

historical_precedents.event: Niger military coup
historical_precedents.what_happened: On 26 July 2023, General Abdourahamane Tchiani led the presidential guard in removing President Mohamed Bazoum and installed a military council. The regional bloc ECOWAS responded with an ultimatum, then sanctions including closed land and air borders, a no-fly zone on commercial flights, suspension of financial transactions, and asset freezes; Nigeria cut electricity supply to Niger on 2 August 2023.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The West African regional central bank cancelled a planned 30 billion CFA franc (about $51 million) bond issuance for Niger, and the World Bank suspended disbursements to the country. Niger is a significant global uranium exporter, and the coup raised questions over the operations of French nuclear fuel company Orano's mining activities there.

historical_precedents.event: Myanmar military coup
historical_precedents.what_happened: Senior General Min Aung Hlaing seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi and other elected officials. The Biden administration imposed sanctions on military leaders on 11 February 2021 and froze $1 billion in Myanmar government assets held in the U.S.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Foreign direct investment into Myanmar fell 22% to $3.8 billion in fiscal year 2020, and major foreign investors withdrew: Japan's Kirin ended a $1.7 billion brewery joint venture, Thailand's Amata halted a $1 billion industrial zone project, and India's Adani Ports terminated a $127 million port investment. The Yangon Stock Exchange suspended trading, and property sales reportedly dropped by nearly 100%.

possibility_chains: A coup in a country that is a significant exporter of a specific commodity has historically raised questions about the continuity of that country's mining, energy, or agricultural exports, even when physical production is not immediately disrupted.
Coups have historically triggered sanctions and suspended aid or financing from regional blocs and international lenders, adding fiscal strain on top of the immediate political disruption.

Foreign companies operating in a country that experiences a coup have historically paused or withdrawn planned investment until the new government's posture toward existing contracts and foreign ownership becomes clearer.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Myanmar military coup (February 2021): Foreign direct investment into Myanmar fell 22% to $3.8 billion in fiscal year 2020, and major foreign investors withdrew: Japan's Kirin ended a $1.7 billion brewery joint venture, Thailand's Amata halted a $1 billion industrial zone project, and India's Adani Ports terminated a $127 million port investment. The Yangon Stock Exchange suspended trading, and property sales reportedly dropped by nearly 100%. A coup in a country that is a significant exporter of a specific commodity has historically raised questions about the continuity of that country's mining, energy, or agricultural exports, even when physical production is not immediately disrupted.

linked_playbooks.name: Sanctions imposed on a major economy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program (2010s): Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods. Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

linked_playbooks.name: Diplomatic rupture between major regional powers
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia severs relations with Iran (January 2016): The rupture deepened the broader Saudi-Iran regional rivalry playing out through proxy conflicts in Yemen, Syria, and elsewhere; relations were not restored until a China-brokered agreement announced 10 March 2023, with embassies reopening in Riyadh in June 2023 and Tehran in August 2023. A sudden severing of diplomatic relations between neighboring major economies has historically disrupted direct trade, aviation, and financial flows between them, forcing rerouting of commerce through third countries at added cost.

linked_playbooks.name: Sharp currency devaluation / currency crisis
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Turkish lira crisis (2018): The lira lost roughly 30–40% of its value against the U.S. dollar over the year, sharply raising the cost of imports and foreign-currency debt for Turkish businesses. A sharp currency devaluation has historically made imported goods, including fuel and food, significantly more expensive for consumers and businesses in the affected country.

ripple_effect.name: Minimum wage policy shift

historical_precedents.event: "Fight for $15" movement
historical_precedents.what_happened: The movement began in November 2012 when over 100 fast-food workers walked off the job in New York City demanding a $15 hourly wage and the right to unionize, at a time when the federal minimum wage had been frozen at $7.25 since 2009; it grew into coordinated multi-city strikes, including an April 2015 day of action across more than 200 cities that organizers called the largest protest by low-wage workers in US history.
historical_precedents.market_impact: By the mid-2020s seventeen US states plus Washington, D.C. had adopted $15-or-higher minimum wages, with organizers estimating roughly 26 million workers received a combined $151 billion in raises traceable to the movement's pressure on state and local policy.

historical_precedents.event: Seattle becomes the first major US city to adopt a $15 minimum wage
historical_precedents.what_happened: Seattle's city council, led by councilmember Kshama Sawant, passed an ordinance phasing in a $15 minimum wage starting in 2014, with the wage rising further to $15.45 in 2018 and $16 in 2019 under the city's indexing formula.
historical_precedents.market_impact: University of Washington and other researchers studying Seattle's rollout found no measurable decline in overall employment as the wage floor rose, making Seattle a frequently cited case study in the broader minimum-wage debate.

possibility_chains: A minimum wage increase in one large city or state has historically prompted advocacy campaigns citing it as precedent for similar increases elsewhere, spreading policy change faster than pure economic modeling alone would predict.

Employers in low-margin, labor-intensive sectors (fast food, retail, hospitality) have historically responded to minimum wage increases through some combination of price increases, reduced hours, and accelerated investment in self-service or automation technology, with the mix varying by study and locality.
Higher minimum wages have historically raised the wage floor workers use as a reference point in unrelated wage negotiations nearby, a "lighthouse effect" observed in several minimum-wage studies.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Seattle becomes the first major US city to adopt a $15 minimum wage (2014–2019): University of Washington and other researchers studying Seattle's rollout found no measurable decline in overall employment as the wage floor rose, making Seattle a frequently cited case study in the broader minimum-wage debate. A minimum wage increase in one large city or state has historically prompted advocacy campaigns citing it as precedent for similar increases elsewhere, spreading policy change faster than pure economic modeling alone would predict.

linked_playbooks.name: Gig-economy worker classification ruling
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: California's Proposition 22 and its multi-year court challenge (November 2020 – July 2024): The nearly four-year legal uncertainty over Proposition 22's validity was itself a business risk for Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, and Instacart, which had spent over $200 million campaigning for the measure; its eventual affirmation cemented independent-contractor status for California gig drivers and became a template gig companies pushed for in other US states. A court or ballot-measure ruling on gig-worker classification in one jurisdiction has historically become a reference point cited by both labor advocates and gig companies lobbying for similar outcomes elsewhere, spreading the policy debate beyond the original jurisdiction.

linked_playbooks.name: Broad-based voluntary quits wave / labor shortage
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: The "Great Resignation" in the United States (March 2021 – mid-2023): Employers responded with the fastest wage growth in two decades — 4.5% year-over-year in December 2021 — while hospitality, healthcare, and education faced acute staffing shortages that pushed many businesses to accelerate investment in automation and self-service technology; quits rates did not return to pre-pandemic 2019 norms until mid-2023. A sustained period of unusually high voluntary quits has historically coincided with faster wage growth, as employers compete harder to retain and attract staff in a tight labor market.

ripple_effect.name: Persian Gulf oil supply shock

historical_precedents.event: Iran–Iraq "Tanker War"
historical_precedents.what_happened: Iran and Iraq attacked oil tankers transiting the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, and Iran repeatedly threatened to close the strait.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Shipping insurance war-risk premiums in the Gulf rose sharply, and the U.S. Navy began escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers in 1987 to keep the strait open.

historical_precedents.event: Drone and missile attack on Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq and Khurais facilities
historical_precedents.what_happened: The attack (which Saudi Arabia and the U.S. blamed on Iran, a claim Iran denied) temporarily knocked out roughly half of Saudi Arabia's oil output, about 5% of global supply.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Brent crude jumped about 15% in a single day — the largest one-day oil price increase since the 1990–91 Gulf War.

historical_precedents.event: Gulf War (Iraqi invasion of Kuwait)
historical_precedents.what_happened: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait removed a large share of Gulf oil exports from the market and raised fears of a wider regional war.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased.

possibility_chains: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.

Because ammonia-based fertilizer production is natural-gas intensive, and natural gas prices often move together with oil, a prolonged energy price spike has historically fed through into higher fertilizer costs over the following months.
Fertilizer is a major input cost in food production, so energy shocks of this kind have historically been followed — often with a lag — by higher food prices.
Shipping insurers have historically raised war-risk premiums for vessels transiting the Gulf during periods of heightened tension, adding to the landed cost of oil and other cargo.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Gulf War (Iraqi invasion of Kuwait) (1990–1991): Oil prices roughly doubled in the months following the invasion before falling back once the war ended and supply concerns eased. Roughly a fifth of the world's oil is estimated to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, so a sustained blockage or major disruption there has historically driven crude oil prices sharply higher.

ripple_effect.name: Broad-based voluntary quits wave / labor shortage

historical_precedents.event: The "Great Resignation" in the United States
historical_precedents.what_happened: A record 47 million Americans voluntarily quit their jobs in 2021 alone, with the monthly quits rate reaching roughly 3% — a level never before recorded since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking it in December 2000 (prior peak 2.4%) — as workers cited wage stagnation, burnout, and inflexible return-to-office policies; food-service quit rates hit 6.8% in October 2021, and about 2.4 million Baby Boomers retired earlier than pre-pandemic trends would have predicted.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Employers responded with the fastest wage growth in two decades — 4.5% year-over-year in December 2021 — while hospitality, healthcare, and education faced acute staffing shortages that pushed many businesses to accelerate investment in automation and self-service technology; quits rates did not return to pre-pandemic 2019 norms until mid-2023.

possibility_chains: A sustained period of unusually high voluntary quits has historically coincided with faster wage growth, as employers compete harder to retain and attract staff in a tight labor market.

Sector-specific quit spikes (hospitality, retail, healthcare during the Great Resignation) have historically prompted employers in those specific sectors to accelerate automation investment, a shift that has typically outlasted the labor shortage that originally motivated it.

A broad wave of voluntary job-switching has historically correlated with a period of unusually strong worker bargaining power, which employer-side surveys and union-organizing activity have both tended to pick up on with a lag of several months.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: The "Great Resignation" in the United States (March 2021 – mid-2023): Employers responded with the fastest wage growth in two decades — 4.5% year-over-year in December 2021 — while hospitality, healthcare, and education faced acute staffing shortages that pushed many businesses to accelerate investment in automation and self-service technology; quits rates did not return to pre-pandemic 2019 norms until mid-2023. A sustained period of unusually high voluntary quits has historically coincided with faster wage growth, as employers compete harder to retain and attract staff in a tight labor market.

linked_playbooks.name: Large-scale tech industry layoffs
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Elon Musk's mass layoffs at Twitter after his acquisition (November 2022 – April 2023): By January 2023 Twitter's headcount had fallen to roughly 2,300, and by April 2023 fewer than 1,500 active employees remained — an approximately 80% reduction from pre-acquisition levels — while the company also faced worker lawsuits alleging inadequate notice under the WARN Act. A wave of layoffs at one large tech employer has historically been followed within months by similar cuts at competitors, as boards and investors reward visible cost discipline during the same macro conditions.

linked_playbooks.name: Retail/warehouse unionization campaign wave
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Starbucks Workers United organizing campaign (December 2021 – ongoing): By mid-2026 over 15,000 workers across 706 Starbucks locations had voted to unionize; Starbucks contested the campaign through captive-audience meetings, firing organizers (leading to repeated NLRB findings of "egregious and widespread" labor-law violations, over 80 documented claims), closing some unionized stores including all locations in Ithaca, NY, and a Supreme Court case that made NLRB-ordered reinstatement of fired workers harder to obtain. A high-profile union election win at one location of a large, multi-site employer has historically triggered a wave of union-election petitions at other locations of the same company within the following months, even without direct coordination between sites.

linked_playbooks.name: Minimum wage policy shift
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Seattle becomes the first major US city to adopt a $15 minimum wage (2014–2019): University of Washington and other researchers studying Seattle's rollout found no measurable decline in overall employment as the wage floor rose, making Seattle a frequently cited case study in the broader minimum-wage debate. A minimum wage increase in one large city or state has historically prompted advocacy campaigns citing it as precedent for similar increases elsewhere, spreading policy change faster than pure economic modeling alone would predict.

ripple_effect.name: South China Sea territorial and shipping dispute

historical_precedents.event: Philippines v. China Permanent Court of Arbitration case
historical_precedents.what_happened: The Philippines brought a case to the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in January 2013 challenging China's expansive 'nine-dash line' claim over most of the South China Sea. The tribunal ruled on 12 July 2016 that China's historic-rights claim had no lawful basis under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that none of the disputed Spratly Islands features qualified as islands generating their own exclusive economic zone.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China rejected the ruling as null and void and continued its island-building and patrol activities in the disputed waters. The ruling did not resolve the underlying dispute, and multiple claimant states (Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Taiwan) continue to assert overlapping claims to parts of the same waters, through which a large share of global seaborne trade transits.

possibility_chains: Escalation of naval or coast guard confrontations in the South China Sea has historically raised shipping insurers' and carriers' attention to route risk in a corridor that carries a very large share of world seaborne trade, given the absence, so far, of a sustained blockade in the disputed waters.

Legal rulings against a claimant state in international tribunals have historically been rejected by the losing party when core territorial claims are involved, meaning such rulings have tended to shape diplomatic and legal leverage over years rather than immediately resolve the dispute.

Long-running territorial disputes in contested waters have historically constrained joint oil and gas exploration in the same areas, since companies are typically reluctant to invest amid unresolved sovereignty claims.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Philippines v. China Permanent Court of Arbitration case (2013–2016): China rejected the ruling as null and void and continued its island-building and patrol activities in the disputed waters. The ruling did not resolve the underlying dispute, and multiple claimant states (Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Taiwan) continue to assert overlapping claims to parts of the same waters, through which a large share of global seaborne trade transits. Escalation of naval or coast guard confrontations in the South China Sea has historically raised shipping insurers' and carriers' attention to route risk in a corridor that carries a very large share of world seaborne trade, given the absence, so far, of a sustained blockade in the disputed waters.

linked_playbooks.name: Critical shipping route disruption
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Houthi attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea (Late 2023 – ongoing): Many major shipping lines rerouted around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding roughly 10–14 days to typical Asia–Europe voyages and pushing container freight rates sharply higher on affected routes. Disruption to a major shipping chokepoint has historically forced vessels onto longer alternate routes, raising fuel and time costs that carriers have often passed on as higher freight rates.

linked_playbooks.name: International court ruling on a territorial or trade dispute
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Philippines v. China South China Sea arbitration (2013–2016): China rejected the ruling outright and continued its activities in the disputed waters, showing that, unlike the Bakassi case where the losing party ultimately complied, an international ruling does not automatically compel compliance from a major power that rejects the tribunal's jurisdiction. International court rulings on territorial or maritime disputes have historically been complied with when the losing government has a political and diplomatic interest in maintaining its standing with the court system, as in the Bakassi case, but have been rejected outright by major powers unwilling to accept binding third-party jurisdiction over sovereignty claims, as in the South China Sea case.

linked_playbooks.name: Taiwan Strait military and political tension
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: China's military exercises following U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan (August 2022): Airlines and shipping operators rerouted some flights and vessels around the announced exercise and exclusion zones surrounding Taiwan for the duration of the drills. Periods of heightened Taiwan Strait tension have historically prompted temporary rerouting of commercial shipping and air traffic around announced exercise or exclusion zones, given Taiwan's location on major East Asia air and sea routes.

ripple_effect.name: Sanctions imposed on a major economy

historical_precedents.event: Western sanctions on Russia following its invasion of Ukraine
historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S., EU, and allies imposed sweeping sanctions on Russia's financial system, energy exports, and access to Western technology, and froze a large share of Russia's foreign-currency reserves.
historical_precedents.market_impact: European natural gas prices spiked to record highs as Russian pipeline gas supply to Europe fell sharply over the following year, and European governments spent heavily to secure alternative energy supplies and shield consumers from higher bills.

historical_precedents.event: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program
historical_precedents.what_happened: A series of U.S. and international sanctions restricted Iran's ability to sell oil and access the global banking system.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods.

possibility_chains: Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

Sanctioned countries have historically sought alternative trading partners and payment systems over time, a process that has typically reduced — but not eliminated — the sanctions' economic impact the longer they remain in place.
Countries or companies that depended heavily on trade with the sanctioned economy have historically faced their own adjustment costs, not just the sanctioned party.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program (2010s): Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods. Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

ripple_effect.name: Retirement age / pension reform and backlash

historical_precedents.event: France's 2023 pension reform and nationwide strikes
historical_precedents.what_happened: The French government proposed raising the legal retirement age from 62 to 64 and increasing the required contribution period from 42 to 43 years; over one million people demonstrated nationwide on January 19, 2023, with subsequent protest days drawing anywhere from several hundred thousand to (by union counts) 2–2.5 million people. On March 16, 2023, Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne invoked Article 49.3 of the constitution to force the bill through without a parliamentary vote, triggering further protests and two no-confidence motions that narrowly failed.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The reform was ultimately enacted despite the sustained opposition, but the government's use of Article 49.3 rather than a parliamentary majority became a lasting point of political controversy, and the episode weighed on President Macron's approval ratings and his coalition's ability to pass subsequent legislation in a parliament where it had already lost its outright majority.

possibility_chains: Government proposals to raise the retirement age have historically triggered some of the largest and most sustained street protests of a given political cycle, since the policy directly and visibly affects a large share of the working population's near-term life plans.

Where a government lacks a legislative majority, forcing a retirement-age or pension reform through by decree or special procedure has historically deepened, rather than resolved, the underlying political conflict, leaving lasting effects on the government's ability to pass unrelated legislation.

Pension and retirement-age reforms have historically interacted with demographic pressure (a shrinking ratio of working-age contributors to retirees) as the underlying economic justification, even when the political debate has focused primarily on fairness and timing.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: France's 2023 pension reform and nationwide strikes (January–June 2023): The reform was ultimately enacted despite the sustained opposition, but the government's use of Article 49.3 rather than a parliamentary majority became a lasting point of political controversy, and the episode weighed on President Macron's approval ratings and his coalition's ability to pass subsequent legislation in a parliament where it had already lost its outright majority. Government proposals to raise the retirement age have historically triggered some of the largest and most sustained street protests of a given political cycle, since the policy directly and visibly affects a large share of the working population's near-term life plans.

linked_playbooks.name: Inflation-driven public-sector/transport strike wave
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: 2022–2024 UK railway strikes (21 June 2022 – November 2024): Strike days cut services to roughly 20% of normal timetabled capacity, and the hospitality sector estimated £1.5 billion in lost trade over the dispute; the UK's Conservative government blocked settlement in England for an extended period even as devolved Scottish and Welsh disputes were resolved by May 2023, with final agreement in England only reached after the 2024 change of government, when workers secured improved pay and the cancellation of proposed ticket-office closures. A period of high inflation eroding real wages has historically produced a wave of strikes across multiple public-facing sectors in the same country within the same one-to-two-year window, rather than an isolated dispute in a single industry.

ripple_effect.name: Disease outbreak with international health emergency

historical_precedents.event: West Africa Ebola outbreak
historical_precedents.what_happened: The World Health Organization declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern as Ebola spread across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone; several airlines suspended routes to the region and some countries imposed travel restrictions.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The World Bank estimated the outbreak cost the three hardest-hit countries over $2 billion in lost economic output.

historical_precedents.event: Zika virus outbreak
historical_precedents.what_happened: The WHO declared a Public Health Emergency as Zika spread across the Americas, linked to birth defects; several countries issued travel advisories affecting tourism, notably ahead of the Rio de Janeiro Olympics.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Tourism-dependent economies in affected regions reported measurable declines in visitor bookings during the advisory period.

possibility_chains: A WHO-declared public health emergency has historically triggered travel advisories and, in some cases, temporary route suspensions by airlines.
Disease outbreaks with international travel warnings have historically reduced tourism and business travel to the affected region for the duration of the advisory.
Outbreaks affecting agricultural or manufacturing regions have historically disrupted local labor supply and production.
Vaccine and treatment developers have historically seen increased investment and expedited regulatory review during major outbreaks.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Zika virus outbreak (2016): Tourism-dependent economies in affected regions reported measurable declines in visitor bookings during the advisory period. A WHO-declared public health emergency has historically triggered travel advisories and, in some cases, temporary route suspensions by airlines.

signals.headline: Jos DisCo Cuts Power Supply To Benue State

ripple_effect.name: Cascading power grid blackout

historical_precedents.event: Northeast blackout of 2003
historical_precedents.what_happened: A software bug in a FirstEnergy alarm system in Ohio failed to alert grid operators that overgrown trees were contacting transmission lines; the resulting failure cascaded across the interconnected grid within minutes, cutting power across the northeastern and midwestern US and Ontario, Canada.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Roughly 55 million people lost power, including 14.3 million in the New York City area, 8.3 million in the Toronto area, and 6.4 million in metropolitan Detroit; the blackout prompted the eventual creation of mandatory, enforceable electric reliability standards in the US and Canada, since none existed at the time of the failure.

possibility_chains: A localized equipment or software fault on a highly interconnected grid has historically cascaded far beyond its origin point, since protective systems designed to isolate faults can also propagate them if operators lose situational awareness in time.

Large-scale blackouts spanning multiple utilities or jurisdictions have historically exposed gaps in coordination and information-sharing between grid operators, prompting regulatory reform after the fact rather than before.

The economic cost of a major blackout has historically scaled with its duration and the concentration of economic activity (manufacturing, finance, transit) in the affected area, rather than simply with the number of people affected.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Northeast blackout of 2003 (14-16 August 2003): Roughly 55 million people lost power, including 14.3 million in the New York City area, 8.3 million in the Toronto area, and 6.4 million in metropolitan Detroit; the blackout prompted the eventual creation of mandatory, enforceable electric reliability standards in the US and Canada, since none existed at the time of the failure. A localized equipment or software fault on a highly interconnected grid has historically cascaded far beyond its origin point, since protective systems designed to isolate faults can also propagate them if operators lose situational awareness in time.

linked_playbooks.name: Winter storm grid failure
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Winter Storm Uri / Texas power crisis (February 2021): Wholesale electricity prices hit the market cap of $9,000 per megawatt-hour (versus a typical $25-50/MWh) and stayed there for roughly two days longer than regulators later found necessary, adding an estimated $16 billion in charges; at least 246 confirmed deaths were attributed to the storm, and total damages reached at least $26.5 billion. A severe cold snap hitting a power grid not designed for extreme winter weather has historically caused simultaneous failures across generation, transmission, and fuel-supply infrastructure, compounding a shortage that any single fix could not solve quickly.

linked_playbooks.name: Electricity market deregulation crisis
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: California electricity crisis (2000-2001): Wholesale electricity prices rose about 800% between April and December 2000; utilities were forced to buy power at 11-50 cents per kilowatt-hour while capped at selling it to consumers at 6.7 cents, and Pacific Gas & Electric filed for bankruptcy in April 2001. Total estimated damage to the California economy reached $40-45 billion. Electricity market designs that cap retail prices while leaving wholesale prices to float have historically left utilities exposed to ruinous losses during supply shortages, since they cannot pass through higher costs to consumers in real time.

linked_playbooks.name: Cyberattack on critical infrastructure
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: NotPetya malware outbreak (June 2017): Maersk had to reinstall its entire global IT infrastructure and briefly ran port terminal operations manually; total global damages were later estimated at over $10 billion, making it one of the most costly cyberattacks in history. A cyberattack that forces critical infrastructure offline (pipelines, ports, power grids) has historically caused localized shortages and price spikes in the directly affected region, even when the underlying supply elsewhere is unaffected.

signals.headline: Audi invertirá 4.000 millones de dólares en su primera fábrica en EEUU tras el impacto de los aranceles de Trump

ripple_effect.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war

historical_precedents.event: U.S.–China trade war
historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. imposed tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese goods, and China retaliated with its own tariffs, including on U.S. agricultural exports.
historical_precedents.market_impact: U.S. soybean exports to China fell sharply, and the U.S. government paid out tens of billions of dollars in subsidies to farmers hurt by the retaliation; global manufacturers reported higher input costs and supply-chain uncertainty through the period.

historical_precedents.event: Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act
historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. raised tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods to some of the highest levels in a century; Canada, France, and other major trading partners retaliated with their own tariffs within months.
historical_precedents.market_impact: World trade volumes fell by roughly two-thirds over the following four years; widely cited by economists as having deepened and prolonged the Great Depression globally, not just in the U.S. — the clearest historical example that a major tariff escalation's damage isn't confined to the two countries directly involved.

historical_precedents.event: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan
historical_precedents.what_happened: After Japan detained a Chinese trawler captain following a collision near the disputed Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands, China informally slowed rare earth mineral shipments to Japan without declaring a formal ban.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling.

possibility_chains: New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.
Retaliatory tariffs targeting a country's agricultural or manufacturing exports have historically hurt the specific industries and regions most exposed to that export market.

Extended periods of tariff uncertainty have historically led some companies to shift or diversify supply chains toward other countries, a process that has typically played out over one to several years, not weeks.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan (September 2010 – 2011): China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling. New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.

signals.headline: ROONEY HAS SHOCKED EVERYONE! And he says this transformation came from HARD WORK, not Ozempic

ripple_effect.name: GLP-1 obesity/diabetes drugs reshaping healthcare cost and pharma markets

historical_precedents.event: Novo Nordisk's Ozempic/Wegovy-driven rise to Europe's most valuable company, then competitive erosion
historical_precedents.what_happened: Demand for Novo Nordisk's GLP-1 drugs Ozempic (approved for diabetes, widely used off-label for weight loss) and Wegovy (approved for obesity) grew so rapidly that weight-loss drugs made up 55% of the company's 2023 revenue and its first-half 2023 profit rose 45% year-over-year; by March 2024 the company reached a $604 billion market capitalization, the 12th most valuable company in the world, and by April 2024 its roughly $570 billion market cap exceeded the size of Denmark's entire economy, with its roughly $2.3 billion Danish corporate tax bill alone driving nearly all of Denmark's measured economic growth that year.
historical_precedents.market_impact: US list prices for these drugs ran far above prices charged elsewhere (Ozempic around $969/month in the US versus $155 in Canada and $59 in Germany; Wegovy around $1,349/month in the US versus $140 in Germany and $92 in the UK), fueling a US health-insurance and employer-benefit-design debate over covering the drugs at scale; by July 2025, rising competitor pressure had pushed Novo down to the fifth most valuable drugmaker by market cap, prompting a CEO change effective August 7, 2025.

possibility_chains: A single drug class becoming a large share of a national economy's growth, as with Novo Nordisk and Denmark, has historically made that country's headline GDP figures unusually sensitive to one company's product cycle.

Insurers and employers facing a costly new high-demand drug class have historically responded first with coverage restrictions (prior authorization, BMI thresholds) before broadening access as production scales and price competition emerges.

A manufacturer's inability to keep pace with demand for a breakout drug has historically triggered shortages, compounding-pharmacy workarounds, and counterfeit-product risk in the gap before supply catches up.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Novo Nordisk's Ozempic/Wegovy-driven rise to Europe's most valuable company, then competitive erosion (2022–2025): US list prices for these drugs ran far above prices charged elsewhere (Ozempic around $969/month in the US versus $155 in Canada and $59 in Germany; Wegovy around $1,349/month in the US versus $140 in Germany and $92 in the UK), fueling a US health-insurance and employer-benefit-design debate over covering the drugs at scale; by July 2025, rising competitor pressure had pushed Novo down to the fifth most valuable drugmaker by market cap, prompting a CEO change effective August 7, 2025. A single drug class becoming a large share of a national economy's growth, as with Novo Nordisk and Denmark, has historically made that country's headline GDP figures unusually sensitive to one company's product cycle.

linked_playbooks.name: Pharmaceutical patent cliff and blockbuster drug revenue loss
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Lipitor (atorvastatin) patent expiration (1996–2012 (US patent expired November 30, 2011)): Generic prices stayed relatively elevated during that initial exclusivity window, then fell sharply once additional manufacturers entered in May 2012, pushing a month's supply down toward standard generic pricing of $10 or less — illustrating the two-stage price collapse (moderate initial generic discount, then a much steeper one once multiple generic makers compete) that characterizes a typical pharmaceutical patent-cliff event. A cluster of blockbuster drugs (defined in the industry as over $1 billion in annual sales) losing patent protection in the same multi-year window has historically pushed large pharmaceutical companies toward M&A, portfolio diversification, and 'evergreening' strategies (new formulations or delivery mechanisms) to offset the revenue drop.

linked_playbooks.name: Aging population driving healthcare system cost and capacity pressure
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Japan's healthcare spending rise under a super-aged population (2008–2018): Japan introduced a dedicated long-term care insurance system (Kaigo-Hoken), funded partly by a roughly 2% income contribution from residents over 40 and administered by municipal governments, specifically to fund elderly care costs separately from general health insurance as the aging-driven cost pressure became structural rather than cyclical; by 2016 the system was allocating tens of billions of dollars annually toward long-term care expenditures. A country crossing the 'super-aged society' threshold (21%+ population 65+) has historically required either new dedicated funding mechanisms, as with Japan's long-term-care insurance, or rising general healthcare spending as a share of GDP, or both.

signals.headline: Response to sardine mortality must be grounded in science and evidence

ripple_effect.name: Overfishing collapses a major wild fishery

historical_precedents.event: Collapse of the Atlantic northwest cod fishery and Canada's fishing moratorium
historical_precedents.what_happened: Decades of overfishing, intensified by industrial trawling from the late 1950s, drove Northern cod stocks off Newfoundland down to about 1% of historic levels. In 1992, Canadian Fisheries Minister John Crosbie declared a moratorium on cod fishing — the largest industrial closure in Canadian history — later extended indefinitely as five more cod stocks also collapsed.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Roughly 35,000–37,000 fishermen and plant workers across more than 400 coastal communities in Newfoundland lost their jobs. The federal government spent heavily on income-support and retraining programs, but cod stocks had still not recovered a decade later; a 2010 study found stocks at only about 10% of their original size. Canada did not lift the moratorium until 2024, when it set a total allowable catch of 18,000 tons for the first time since 1992.

possibility_chains: A wild fishery collapse driven by overfishing has historically taken decades, not years, to show meaningful recovery, unlike many crop-yield shocks that can reverse within a single growing season.

Fishing communities dependent on a single collapsed stock have historically faced prolonged, structural unemployment rather than a temporary downturn, given how few alternative wild fisheries exist nearby.

Fishery collapses have historically prompted governments to impose strict, sometimes indefinite, catch moratoria — a policy tool with far fewer parallels in crop agriculture, where land can typically be replanted the following season.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Collapse of the Atlantic northwest cod fishery and Canada's fishing moratorium (1992, effects ongoing for decades): Roughly 35,000–37,000 fishermen and plant workers across more than 400 coastal communities in Newfoundland lost their jobs. The federal government spent heavily on income-support and retraining programs, but cod stocks had still not recovered a decade later; a 2010 study found stocks at only about 10% of their original size. Canada did not lift the moratorium until 2024, when it set a total allowable catch of 18,000 tons for the first time since 1992. A wild fishery collapse driven by overfishing has historically taken decades, not years, to show meaningful recovery, unlike many crop-yield shocks that can reverse within a single growing season.

linked_playbooks.name: El Niño-driven fishery collapse disrupts a major protein and feed source
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Another major El Niño again reduces the Peruvian anchoveta population (1997–1998): The renewed decline negatively affected Peru's fisheries and the broader economy, underscoring the anchoveta fishery's recurring vulnerability to El Niño cycles even after the 1972 collapse. Because anchovy caught off Peru is one of the world's largest single sources of fish used to produce fishmeal for animal feed and aquaculture, a major collapse in that fishery has historically raised concern among fishmeal-dependent industries about feed costs, even though the exact size of any resulting price move has varied by episode.

linked_playbooks.name: Post-Brexit fishing rights dispute threatens trade retaliation
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: 2021 Jersey fishing dispute between France and the UK/Jersey (April–September 2021, into 2022): About 250 French fishing boats and roughly 900 families/2,000 jobs in Normandy and Brittany were affected by the licensing restrictions. The UK deployed Royal Navy patrol vessels in response to the blockade, and the dispute remained only partially resolved into 2022, with Jersey gradually increasing the number of permanent licenses it issued. Post-Brexit fishing-access disputes have historically escalated quickly from a narrow licensing disagreement into threats against unrelated sectors, such as energy supply or financial-services access, reflecting how interconnected small, dependent economies can be with their neighbors.

signals.headline: Peste porcine africaine : les éleveurs réclament le paiement de leurs indemnités

ripple_effect.name: African swine fever outbreak collapses China's pork supply

historical_precedents.event: African swine fever spreads across China's pig herd
historical_precedents.what_happened: China's first confirmed case of African swine fever was reported in Liaoning province in August 2018 (with more than 38,000 hogs culled within the first two weeks); within about eight months the disease had spread to every region of China. China's pig population fell by almost 100 million head compared with the previous year — roughly a quarter of the global pig population affected. The disease also spread through Southeast Asia, reaching Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The resulting pork supply shortage pushed China to sharply increase pork imports, and European pork prices reached a six-year high as international demand rose to help fill the gap left by China's collapsed domestic production.

possibility_chains: A livestock disease outbreak in the world's largest producer/consumer of a given meat has historically reshaped global trade flows for that commodity, pulling imports from exporting countries and raising prices in those export markets too.

Countries hit by a major livestock epidemic have historically accelerated biosecurity investment and herd-rebuilding programs, a process that has typically taken multiple years to restore pre-outbreak production levels.

A large, sudden loss of one protein source has historically shifted consumer demand toward substitute proteins (e.g. poultry, beef, or soy-based products) in the affected country, with knock-on price effects in those markets.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: African swine fever spreads across China's pig herd (August 2018 – 2019): The resulting pork supply shortage pushed China to sharply increase pork imports, and European pork prices reached a six-year high as international demand rose to help fill the gap left by China's collapsed domestic production. A livestock disease outbreak in the world's largest producer/consumer of a given meat has historically reshaped global trade flows for that commodity, pulling imports from exporting countries and raising prices in those export markets too.

linked_playbooks.name: Avian influenza outbreak drives poultry and egg price shock
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) forces mass culling of U.S. egg-laying hens (2022 onward): The mass culling sharply reduced the U.S. egg-laying flock and was followed by 'skyrocketing' egg prices, a pattern that recurred with further culling waves in subsequent years; egg producers such as Cal-Maine later faced scrutiny, including litigation over pricing coordination between 2022 and 2025, during the shortage period. A major livestock disease outbreak that forces large-scale culling has historically produced protein-specific price spikes (e.g. eggs or poultry) within months, distinct from broader crop-driven food inflation.

linked_playbooks.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan (September 2010 – 2011): China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling. New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.
